coverage.assessment: The Beethoven and Thuringen setups are grounded in 007. Two connectives lost their antecedents: 'Suddenly' (P6) and 'Yet Gibbon' (P21).
Locations stay inferable after the Valtellina cut. Kuhns, Palmer, Chandler and Browning are clearly identified. The barricade-to-Mals sequence is intact.
The only performed line, "Sir, I am a tourist!", is intact. The Garibaldi talk remains reported, as in the source.

The 'Not that Adams felt any real doubt' qualifier and the 'good were robbed' hinge are cut. Seward support, chronology and the speculative 'failure of a third' are preserved, and the Garibaldi Autobiography line was removed rather than misstated.
Several markers separating the young man's ignorance from the old narrator's hindsight were removed. There is no premature disclosure of the sister's fate or of Lincoln.
The ledger tone and aphorisms survive. The Milan meditation lost its 'half-a-dozen such' rhythm, a defensible but real cost.
Rome's contradiction with a cause-seeking education and the sister's role in settling the moral question are weakened.
Ara Coeli, the sister and the Palermo dependencies are intact at both ends. The King plant was an authorized cut, and the 022 partner introduces King self-sufficiently.

dependencies.assessment: The local Gibbon quotation and the sunset Ara Coeli musing are concrete. The 035 partner keeps the breakdown on the steps, and there is no anticipation of the dynamic theory.

findings.claim: The revision cuts 'Not that Adams felt any real doubt about his sympathies…the moment was decisive…for political morals'. It also cuts 'it might happen that the good were robbed'. P8 now jumps from 'take sides first' straight to steam and electricity.
findings.counterevidence: The essential question 'when and why robbery and murder were a virtue' and V1 survive.

evidence.quote: Not that Adams felt any real doubt about his sympathies or wishes.
but it might happen that the good were robbed.
Not that Adams felt any real doubt about his sympathies or wishes, but the moment was decisive for much to come, especially for political morals.
His morals were the highest, and he clung to them to preserve his self-respect; but steam and electricity had brought about new political and social concentrations

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first-draft opening sentence of P8 and the clause 'As long as he could argue…the good were robbed.'
findings.reader_effect: The source distinguishes settled sympathies from an unsettled moral foundation. Without the qualifier, Adams seems genuinely torn. Without the 'good were robbed' step, the monkey sentence loses the case that forces it.
findings.title: Moral-dilemma qualifier and robbery hinge removed

findings.claim: The revision cuts the generalization that women's will 'ends by settling the moral'. It also cuts her wish to have him 'civilized' rather than 'Germanized'. 'Luckily for him' therefore no longer resolves the preceding unanswered question.
findings.counterevidence: V2 and the vivid character catalogue remain, so the sister stays bright and dominant.

evidence.quote: Women have, commonly, a very positive moral sense; that which they will, is right; that which they reject, is wrong; and their will, in most cases, ends by settling the moral.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'Women have, commonly…settling the moral' sentence from the first draft.
findings.plan_relation: planning omission: the plan protects V2 but not this sentence, which links the moral dilemma to the reins and the general law
findings.reader_effect: In the source, Mrs. Kuhn's positive will settles the moral question he cannot. Without that link, the sister section reads as a new topic. Her decisive character is also slightly thinned.

findings.minimal_repair: Reinstate the first-draft sentence before 'Yet Gibbon'.

findings.reader_effect: In the source, Browning is a possible companion for Gibbon who still could not explain Rome. Without the bridge, the anecdote feels detached, and 'Yet' reads as a non sequitur.

findings.claim: Three markers kept in the first draft are gone in the revision: 'Of the Germany to come, he knew nothing', 'The thought of posing for a Gibbon never entered his mind', and the after-life shame over the Courier letters.
findings.counterevidence: Other retrospective cues survive, such as 'In after life he made a general law' and 'never again felt quite the old confident charm'.

evidence.quote: Of the Germany to come, he knew nothing.

He had little to say, and said it not very well; but it was still the nearest approach he had yet made to an intelligent act.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore at least the two short sentences 'Of the Germany to come…' and 'The thought of posing for a Gibbon…'.
findings.reader_effect: The voice profile requires keeping the young man's beliefs distinct from the old man's judgments. These lines carry the dramatic irony. Their loss pushes the text toward flat narration and undercuts the ironic weight of 'nearest approach…to an intelligent act'.

findings.claim: The revision drops the clause about young men 'taking for granted that everything had a cause, and that nature tended to an end'. That clause made Rome 'the most violent vice in the world'. Only 'seductive beyond resistance' remains.
findings.counterevidence: V4 and P18's 'No law of progress applied to it' still carry the thesis in part.

findings.reader_effect: This clause sets up why Rome defeats any law of progress or sequence in P18 and the 'Why!!!' at Ara Coeli. Without it, Rome is merely charming rather than an affront to a causal education.

findings.counterevidence: P5 still states his love of an eighteenth-century, mediaeval Germany.

findings.claim: The revision cuts 'Life had no richer impression to give; it offers barely half-a-dozen such, and the intervals seem long.' The exchangeable-value sentence now follows 'ends attained' directly.
findings.counterevidence: The essential pleasure/pain line and the Beethoven comparison remain.

Life had no richer impression to give; it offers barely half-a-dozen such, and the intervals seem long.

findings.reader_effect: The sentence gives the attainment its emotional scale before the mock-economic turn. The argument survives, but its pacing and melancholy are thinner.
findings.title: Milan meditation loses its 'half-a-dozen' cadence

strengths: All eight verbatim passages are preserved exactly, including the typographic 'Why! Why!! Why!!!' escalation and the glow-worm deflation.
The Stelvio sequence keeps the uncertainty, the Ortler barricade with gun barrels lost in snow, Mrs. Kuhn's gasp, and the loss of German charm at Mals.
The Garibaldi scene keeps its framing as 'knowledge of one's ignorance of men' and the sphinx/red-shirt portrait unread.
The Paris coda preserves the paradox of disapproval licensing enjoyment and closes on 'mixed emotions but no education'.
summary: The revision keeps every essential episode and all eight verbatim passages. The supplied dependencies hold. Its new cuts, beyond the first draft, remove several hinge sentences: the qualifier on Adams's moral doubt, the link between women's will and the moral dilemma, the Browning–Gibbon bridge, Rome's 'violent vice' premise, the 'worlds passed and worlds coming' transition, and several retrospective-distance markers. None breaks the chapter. Together they flatten its argumentative joints and its old-man/young-man irony, so each warrants a small editorial restoration.
